newsitem.title: UK: YEAREND - Football came home, but Estonia went missing.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Football came home, but Estonia went missing.

text.p: Football came home to its birthplace in the summer of 1996 but it was Germany not England who were celebrating loudest and longest at the end of the major event of the year -- the European Championship.

England was transformed for three heady weeks in June as Euro 96 gripped the nation's imagination in a way no sports event had done in the home of the game since England hosted the World Cup 30 years ago.
The ideal finale to the championship would have been England winning, as they did in 1966.

Instead, millions of distraught English men, women and children suffered the agonies of seeing their team lose to Germany on a penalty shoot-out in the semifinals of a major championship for the second time in six years.
In Italy in 1990 the Germans knocked England out of the World Cup on penalties, and they did the same again at Wembley on the night of June 26.

Berti Vogts' team then went on to beat the Czech Republic 2-1 in the final at Wembley four days later, courtesy of a controversial sudden-death "golden goal" scored by Oliver Bierhoff four minutes into extra time.

It was the first time a major title had been decided in such a way and, while it gave Germany a deserved third European title, the debate still rages about the best way to decide matches level after 90 minutes in championship football.
OFF TO A GOOD START, BUT KNOCKOUT DISAPPOINTING

For while the opening group stage of Euro 96 was peppered with bright, flowing games, the knockout section was a disappointment with two of the four quarter-finals decided by penalties as well as both semifinals.
The sport's governing bodies have yet to find a fairer way of concluding games and, until they do, major championships are likely to be settled in this unsatisfactory manner.

Still, not all Englishmen were disappointed this summer. England striker Alan Shearer ended Euro 96 as the tournament's top striker with five goals and a month later moved from Blackburn Rovers to Newcastle United for a world record fee of 15 million sterling ($25 million).
BOSMAN RULING A WATERSHED

Plenty of overseas players -- taking full advantage of the December 1995 Bosman ruling which allowed players to become free agents at the end of their contracts and did away with restrictions on the number of foreign players in any one team -- flocked to England.
Top Italians swarmed in with Fabrizio Ravanelli moving to unfashionable Middlesbrough and his former Juventus team mate Gianluca Vialli going to Chelsea, as did Gianfranco Zola of Parma.
The barriers on cross-border transfers crumbled in 1996 as a result of the Bosman ruling and the year will be seen as a watershed in the history of European soccer.
SIGNIFICANT YEAR FOR AFRICA
While Euro 96 dominated much of European football, the year was also a significant one for Africa with the South Africans hosting and winning their continental championship in January.
Nigeria then stunned most observers by winning the Olympic soccer title, while Liberian George Weah of AC Milan inherited Diego Maradona's crown and mantle of the best player in the world.
FOOTBALL TRAGEDIES
But the year was not without tragedy and 81 fans were killed in October before the start of a World Cup qualifying game between Guatamala and Costa Rica.
The disaster was chillingly similar to the Hillsborough tragedy of 1989 when 96 fans were crushed to death in an overcrowded, fenced-in section of terracing in Sheffield, England.
That led FIFA, world soccer's governing body, to call for the removal of all perimeter fencing -- a possible problem for the 1998 World Cup organisers as fencing is required by law in France.
Another tragedy left nine dead following a stampede at a World Cup qualifier between Zambia and Sudan in Lusaka in June.
OTHER EVENTS
At club level Juventus were crowned European champions for the first time in 10 years and went on to win the World Club Cup against South American champions River Plate in Tokyo.
Manchester United created history in England by becoming the first club to win a second league and cup double. In Spain Atletico Madrid also achieved a double.

While the lasting memory of 1996 may well be that of German captain Juergen Klinsmann lifting the European Championship trophy high above his head in June, at least two other images made a deep impression.
The sight and sounds of orange-bedecked Dutch brass bands brought vigour and colour to the stadiums of Euro 96.

The appearance of one of those bands at halftime in the Euro 96 final between Germany and the Czech Republic at Wembley symbolised more than anything the huge changes that have taken place in England, which has virtually rid itself of the hooligan scourge of the 1970s and 1980s. Their contribution to Euro 96 was truly memorable.

And to prove once again that football really is "a funny old game", one need look no further than the events of October 9 in Tallinn, when Estonia failed to show up for a World Cup qualifier against Scotland.
The Scots were all there and kicked off against non- existent opponents before the match was abandoned after only three seconds.

Hundreds of Scottish fans, laughing off the insanity of having travelled across Europe to see a match that never took place, got hold of a ball and played among themselves on the pitch after their bemused team went back to the changing room.
Soccer may be more sleek and sophisticated than ever before but the Dutch brass bands and the Scottish fans showed it is still the game of the people.
